utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUGGE
utterances.text: Good morning. First of all, I would like to inform the parties that Judge Parker is not sitting today. The Chamber nevertheless decided, pursuant to Rule 15 bis (A), that the hearing continues in his absence. Could the witness be brought in.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUGGE
utterances.text: Good morning. Please sit down. I would like to remind you that the affirmation you made at the beginning of your evidence still applies. I'm sure Mr. Djordjevic has still some questions for you. Please, Mr. Djordjevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUGGE
utterances.text: We don't get any translation at the moment.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Can you hear us now?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUGGE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Djordjevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. [Interpretation] I would now like to ask to have Exhibit P455 on our screens.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Professor, this is a table. I would like to tell you that this was done by anthropologist Jose-Pablo Baraybar. He made this table to reflect directly the findings provided by your team and by some other teams. You will see underneath the table Ba, D, PS. That's what is written there. Now I would like to ask you about Ba, that's Batajnica. D is another site, PS is Petrovo Selo, yet another location. But now I would like to ask you only as regards the first table. The grey column refers to the total number of cases. Those were all the bodies that were found in Batajnica. It's obvious that it covers Batajnica 1, Batajnica 2. The darker column refers to the number of deaths that were determined -- in fact, this is not a good translation. It's the number of cases where the cause of death was determined. And finally we have the number of deaths where the cause of death was not determined. According to the findings of your team signed by your associates and also first and foremost by you, you have already explained that the cause of death in accordance with the doctrine that is in place - and you told us that the doctrine that applies is primarily the German doctrine, where it -- when it comes to determining the cause and manner of death - and invoking this doctrine you explained to all of us here that in light of the state of the bodies that were found there and the degree of putrefaction, it was impossible to determine the cause of death. How do you then explain the high percentage of cases in which cause of death was determined in relation to what your team was doing? You will agree that the difference is really immense.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Can I answer? This is the first time that I see this, this chart, or rather, this table. And -- well, my comments will deal with two aspects. The first aspect is that the forensic medical expert -- as forensic medical experts who did the autopsies, we abided by all the tenets, the valid doctrine that is accepted throughout the world, and that is that only hard evidence and facts that have been established can lead to a conclusion about the cause of death. In other words, between the conclusion as to the cause of death and the autopsy, there has to be a consistent link, and that's what is important. Now, having recourse to other information, as I did and as the court does, is yet another form of expert knowledge and it can point to a certain way in which injuries were inflicted and death was caused. As a forensic pathologist performing an autopsy, I have to explain all the items that I found, all the phenomena; and I have to establish a causal relationship with the cause of death so that there is a consistency. And I explained to you last time that the consistency between the conclusion and the findings have to be -- there has to be consistency. And this is presented to the Court, and it is only the Court that has enough relevant information to be able to say, Well, Doctor, this is what you found. And now we have witness testimony, people who saw things, gave evidence, investigative bodies found some elements at the scene, and then all these facts, all this evidence, together with our autopsy findings, can enable an expert to conclude or to predict with greater or lesser probability what the cause of death might be. So there can only be a probability, and this is what is presented to the Court. Now, in -- what facts did I have at my disposal regarding the Batajnica case, not as an expert but as a person performing the exhumation and the autopsies, and this pertains to 2001 in Batajnica and to all the other cases that are dealt with in 1998 in Kosovo at Radonjic Lake; and the findings there were identical to these ones. And all the teams in the territory of the Republic of Serbia provided the same kind of reports or findings regarding putrefied bodies. So what facts did I have? I had the fact that the bodies had been bought there from somewhere else; that they had been transported using various vehicles or means of transport; that some of them had been buried elsewhere, before; and that those persons were killed in various clashes between the terrorist forces, the KLA actions targeting the police and the regular military; and these are all the facts that I had in my head. So there is a high probability that injuries could have been caused in a number of sites, in a variety of ways. And I as a forensic expert, I come to a place where there are bodies who had come there from various places with varying degrees of decomposition and I have to determine the cause of death. And I have no parameters to help me determine what injuries were caused before death and which were caused post mortem. And post mortem and ante mortem injuries look more or less the same. And once the soft and hard tissues start decomposing and once the putrefaction sets in, it is very difficult to determine whether an injury was caused ante mortem or post mortem. And this is why, in forensic practice, in forensic science, this phrase is used, that the body is in an advanced stage of putrefaction and cause of death could not be determined. Now, why Jose-Pablo Baraybar determined the cause of death for 506 cases? Well, first of all, I cannot contest it. I don't know how he explained that away. But first of all, he's an anthropologist. He couldn't have done that without cooperating with a pathologist. He couldn't have done that without having recourse to additional information and without conducting additional analyses on the material that he had. But I can say something else, and I am duty-bound to do so because I have taken a solemn declaration as a witness. I testified as an expert in the Srebrenica seven case, and I had an opportunity to go through the autopsy reports for a large number of people, and those reports were produced by a number of various teams, and this forensic aspect, this is something that Mr. John Clark was talking about. He was one of the key forensic scientists in Srebrenica, and he said more or less the same thing that I did. And then, at one point, he said that one should take, as a starting point, some assumptions as to how these people were killed, assumptions, and then he listed the assumptions that now indicated that it was possible that those people -- the death of those people was actually linked with the events in Srebrenica. I made some comments regarding that, but it's not -- it's immaterial what actually said. But I did come across a very important fact and that's the fact that when the work in Srebrenica started in 1996 - let me just consult my notes - I think it was in 1996, San Antonio was in 1998. Robert Kitchener who was a medical doctor, a member of the Physicians For Human Rights, it's an organisation - and he was the key person overseeing all the forensic work and exhumations in Srebrenica - and Mr. Peter McCloskey a Prosecutor from this Tribunal, the two of them talked to their colleagues, pathologists, forensic experts such as myself, and simply changed the conclusions. And William Haglund testified that in several of his reports. They wanted the conclusions to be drafted in a certain way after exhumations and autopsies, in the same way in which Jose-Pablo Baraybar did, he joined in later on. And as regards those anthropologists' forensic conclusions, if I may call them that, I heard of them a long time before I came here to testify, that meant that he could deal with all the exhumation cases. And then we forensic experts talked among each other and we said, Well, how can he do that without knowing all the details? And that is why I mentioned a man who tried to kill himself by shooting himself in the head. Had that person died a year after this incident, let's say if he had poisoned himself by overdosing on some medication, if he were to be buried and then if an anthropologist were to exhume him and look at him and if you were not aware of any other circumstances, you would draw completely wrong conclusions, and this is the same case as here in Kosovo. I had cases in Kosovo with people dying -- being killed between April and September, over a long time-period in various sites under various circumstances. And we could not determine the cause of death in a single case because of putrefaction, and now to claim that some injuries were caused -- were actually gun-shot wounds, and if you have a body with a gun-shot wound to the pelvis and no head, how can you then guarantee that this person did not have their head cut off first and then was shot in the pelvis? That would have been a major cause of death. But this is why we don't present this to the Court because the Court has all the facts based on the evidence of witnesses and other evidence, and then a realistic conclusion can be drawn with a realistic assumption as to the cause of death. Well, that's the only comment I can make, but I am quite clear as to why he actually wrote this.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: I would just put again on the record that this witness was now a second time asked about the work of another witness, and in so far an opinion was asked from this witness, and he, our witness today, has been invited as a fact witness and the graphic which was just put to him a moment ago is to a certain extent also a complex graphic, requires certain background understanding. And this witness has said that he now for the first time saw this graphic. And I therefore think this is not an appropriate course of action. This is here a scientific product which has been put to this expert which would require a certain explanation, and we are dealing with a fact witness here today. So I don't think it's appropriate to elicit certain opinions from this witness. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUGGE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Neuner. Mr. Djordjevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I think that your colleague, His Honour Judge Parker, together with the rest of the Trial Chamber, has already ruled on such objections. This is a witness who is here testifying about facts that have direct bearing on his work. The questions that I'm asking him I think will assist us all to a great extent in order to determine the facts, to get at the truth. I agree that we can set aside the witness's opinions, but we have to bear in mind that we have here in the courtroom a witness who testified, either as a Prosecution witness or as an expert witness called by the Defence, and has provided opinions that have been invaluable for various Trial Chambers, and that is why I cannot agree with what my learned friend Mr. Neuner is saying.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUGGE
utterances.text: The Chamber very carefully listened to the testimony of this witness and also to the comment of Mr. Neuner - and, please, Mr. Djordjevic, take into account the comment and carry on.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. I fully understand my colleague, Mr. Neuner, but with all due respect I will try to find a way to continue my examination of this witness --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUGGE
utterances.text: Please carry on.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- in the most appropriate way.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: In order to save some time for re-direct, I will tell you that Jose-Pablo Baraybar had forensic medical experts on his team. That's what I wanted to tell you. But what we all know and what we've all seen from the documents that you have provided us, that you signed, in your team you also had a forensic anthropologist or forensic anthropologists or anthropologists. What I have just told you, does that change your opinion or can you tell us something else?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, I will tell you that the anthropologists that we used, Professor Dr. Marija Djuric, unlike Jose-Pablo Baraybar, who is also an anthropologist, Marija Djuric is a medical doctor, she teaches anatomy, and her subspecialty is forensic anatomy. So this is a vital difference. It's a different education than anthropologists have. So she teaches anatomy at the medical school, that's by way of an explanation. And secondly, if this chart, or rather, if when cause of death was being determined, it also involved -- this exercise involved also forensic pathologists, such as myself, then it is less likely to be accurate if they relied only on autopsy reports. In my lengthy explanation I told you who actually came up with this solution in 1996 in Srebrenica and who pursued the same path after that time. In order to be completely clear, in our judicial proceedings in our country, if it is established that a person was killed in certain circumstances and the judge orders an exhumation, we exhume the body and we determine that there are some injuries; and then we conclude, just as we have here, that the cause of death could not be determined and so on and so forth. However, in light of the facts that the investigative judge and the Prosecution give us as experts, for instance, that there was a traffic accident or -- we have the medical charts and all the rest, but due to some circumstances the cause of death was not established, now having recourse to the same facts that the court has, I can provide my opinion, not my findings, to the court and tell the court that in light of all the facts that have been determined and the autopsy report, where I have not been able to determine accurately the cause of death, I can provide my opinion as to whether the injury is linked with the traffic accident in question or not. And to explain whether some injuries that are present could or could not have been caused in the traffic accident. Well, this is what they used here, they provided an opinion based solely on the autopsy report. So a person -- so if you have in front of you a case from Batajnica, let's take it as an example, a through-and-through gun-shot wound to the head which was determined in the course of the autopsy. We said that the body was in an advanced stage of decomposition and that the cause of death could not be determined, full stop; and that is consistent with the findings. If you say that the death of that person is linked to the through-and-through gun-shot wound to the head, that this might be the possible cause of death, I will now posit a different theory and I will say, Yes, there is a through-and-through wound to the head, but this person also had stab wounds to the abdomen or the throat was slit which is why the soft tissue decomposed fairly quickly because it was already damaged and this person bled out quickly; but in order to make sure that this person is dead they also fired a shot to his head. Well, it is also a viable assumption. It is based on the same findings, facts that were established in the course of the autopsy. I know as a forensic expert that this happened. Bodies were desecrated in Kosovo. After all the events, they were desecrated, they were moved from one site to another. The bodies -- well, hand-grenades were thrown on people who were already dead, and this caused additional injuries. So you can't say -- you can't state that this was an ante mortem injury. These are terrible assumptions, dangerous assumptions, unfounded assumptions. That's what I wanted to say.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. My next question that I would like to ask you is: Do you have any knowledge and experience in the area of the former Yugoslavia relating to the way in which persons sustained injuries, and by that I mean whether they were shot from a pistol or from a gun or a rifle or had they sustained shrapnel wounds. Were you able to establish a correlation between such injuries and the fact that these persons had taken part in combat, had been armed, or were unarmed but only on the basis of the information that you have and that is the method of how injuries were caused?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did. And unfortunately I was involved in these examinations, both as an expert and both as a physician. I mentioned the case of Radonjic Lake where for the most part rifles and guns were used, and that was preceded most probably by torture of the victims. As an expert, I worked in 1994 and 1995 on the Derventa cases, where 20 dead people were discovered who were killed regrettably in the same way and by applying the same means as in the Second World War. I was also involved in the work in Srebrenica and Bosnia in general. There are certain characteristics that are -- can be characterised and that can serve to identify which weapon was used to be shot. I'm not saying to be killed but just to be shot. You have to examine the wounds, whether there are entry and exit wounds, et cetera. Therefore, on the basis of that, one may assume whether this person was in a combat activity or it was lined up and shot dead, whether it died -- he died in a war conflict. It is very difficult to establish on the basis of only this information if you don't have additional information. In 1999 we had elderly people in Radonjicko Jezero --

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Sorry to interrupt you, professor, now that you mentioned Radonjic Jezero, why did you investigate Radonjic Jezero who the victims were?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'll tell you just briefly. 1998, in July and August, both Albanians and Serbs were killed at Radonjic Lake by the terrorist organisation KLA. That was the site of execution. But in the period from May on August, they had been captured at various locations and that is where the KLA killed them. There was this concrete canal with the traces of bullets, also some cartridges were found. What I want to say, these victims sustained such wounds that once you see them, you see that there is and entry and exit wound in the chest cavity or abdomen. You can see how they sustained these injuries. We work by establishing the type, the size, and the nature of the injury, and then we can decide which implement was used to cause these injuries, whether it was shrapnel or a bullet, and also we can determine under which circumstances this person died. So, unfortunately, yet again, I have vast experience in these kind of examinations.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: You spoke about Batajnica Jedan and Batajnica Dva, can you tell us what conclusions you drew based on that?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what you mean.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: With respect to the people and the injuries they sustained, whether the injuries were more common on the bones rather than on the soft tissue, et cetera. And on the basis of that, are you able to draw any conclusion as to the way in which these people died, whether they were shot dead or whether -- or whether that was impossible to determine at all.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, let me tell you that I didn't become engaged in this kind of analysis. We didn't establish the number of persons who had any sort of traces of wounds inflicted by fire-arms. We didn't divide them into categories as according to the type of wounded -- wounds that they sustained. That requires additional analysis of clothing and other items found on the spot. What I still don't know to this date, I don't know where these people had come from. They have been identified as people from Kosovo, but at the same time my colleague who testified in the Milutinovic case was in Kosovo. I was her teacher and I was her tutor. When she testified she said that she would do two or three post mortem analyses or the analysis of ten bodies in a day, but all of this was happening during the NATO bombing from -- which lasted from March to June 1999. She would tell me that if they came to the same location two days later she would say that there were no bodies. I asked her how come and she said, We were just about to bury them but we came under fire, we had to retreat. Although she had a huge security detail escorting her in order to enable her to prepare reports and things. So the bodies disappeared the following days. They were obviously removed by the Albanians, and they buried them in larger graves. And why was that done? It is quite clear. When you have five or six bodies to carry out post mortem of and after the visual examination is completed, they are moved to another location where you have 35 bodies. And the point and the aim was to create as big mass graves as possible. Now, if somebody's moving a dead body for a specific purpose, I only can assume that this person could have shot at these dead bodies as well in order to confuse the issue and therefore make it impossible for any anthropologist or pathologist to determine when the wound is inflicted on such a skeletonised body. So these things happened and I have such reports. Therefore, what I told you, that the proper forensic school applies, is that cause of death is impossible to establish. I believe that the Court has information from the spot and that they can fit into this post mortem findings, saying that some people died from fire-arms, some people died from blunt instrument, et cetera. And there were fractures everywhere. There was not a single body without a fracture. Now, they could have been inflicted during beating up, they could be caused by physical force, they could have be caused while loading or unloading into the trucks, or even during the burial or excavation. So we have instances when people were exhumed and transported to Batajnica and reburied again, and then a bulldozer comes to level the ground and can cause hundreds more fractures. So how am I to determine when these things happened and what the time-line is?

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Professor, since you mentioned the bone fractures inflicted after death, is it still possible to determine that some of them really occurred post mortem, for instance, as a result of the weight of the land, of the earth, that was piled upon them?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There are certain characteristics between ante mortem and post mortem fractures. On the face of it, they are very similar; however, to claim that something was caused ante mortem, that is to say before death, it has to have certain characteristics in both soft and hard tissues. This is my answer to your question. The exhumed bodies with the advanced stage of putrefaction show very little or almost no such features. So we can only assume that the body was broken by a dull instrument or a blunt instrument. And if you have transportation and other activities involved, it is difficult to make this distinction.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: My next question speaking of these matters, when you worked in Batajnica 1 and Batajnica 2 did you come up -- come across any traces of attempts to totally destroy the mortal remains?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, there were such traces in Batajnica 1, indicating partial 'destruction' of bodies. I say destruction in inverted commas. There were gun-shots and conditions were created for the most of the bodies to be burned. In other words, in a large number of bodies that we found, we saw traces indicating that they had been exposed to high temperatures in Batajnica.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: But the remains were found, yes?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they were.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: There were about 39 bodies in that grave?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Now, after all this, is it fair to conclude that with regards to the way in which these people were killed and with respect to a possible cause of death, the feasible conclusions were only at the level of probability?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, there was a certain degree of probability.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. My next question concerns something that I as a layperson managed to understand but who else am I to ask this question of but a man who has been living all his life in the Balkans and in the former Yugoslavia. And the question is as follows: Are there any standards for determining the age of a dead body, since in this courtroom we heard that the American standards were applied and that subsequently it was necessary to take the mortal remains of about 800 people to be taken to Tennessee and the Tennessee forensic researchers at their congress in Dallas concluded that there are certain standards applicable to the Balkans populations. Can you tell me, did these standards exist at the time or do they exist when it comes to determining the age or tempore exitus?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, there are standards.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Professor, are these medieval standards?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no. They're not medieval standards. They're generally acceptable standards from the 20th century or late 19th century. We do know some features and we do know some features that make it possible to determine the sex, the age, and the height. Now, as to the estimates of sex and age, there are some numerical parameters that are used as standards for a certain population in a certain area. Americans used the standards that they determined in Vietnam and it was mostly the black population, the soldiers who were killed there, and then they did the numerical analysis and came up with the statistical average -- averages. They already had -- they already knew the height, age, and sex of those victims. And now for the Balkans, the populations in the Balkans, you have to apply certain standards. We had those anthropological standards that had been in use for a long time before Batajnica and all the other events in the former Yugoslavia happened. We had the standards that had been in use in Europe and in Russia. We knew that there were minute differences in the estimates. So the population in the Balkans is not different from the European population. Perhaps there is a slight discrepancy if you compare it with the northern -- with northern Europe where people are taller than they are in the south of Europe. So there are different standards there, but we're somewhere in the middle in the Balkans, and we use the central European standards in making our estimates. So all our analysis are done with the standards, and a colleague of mine and myself we even wrote a paper, it was published in the Journal of Forensic Science.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: So in other words, you informed the scientific public about it?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, in a way.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: My next question with regard to this, you mentioned the visit of anthropologist Baraybar to your institute. I put it to you that there was an agreement on cooperation between the OMPF and our organs where you were supposed to exchange information but also scientific experience. You said you were not aware of it and that it didn't happen. Now, here's my question: Did Jose-Pablo Baraybar ever ask you any questions about the standards that we have been talking about now, so the ones that are used to determine the age of the bodies at the time of death?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, believe me, I can't now testify -- well, there was a discussion with the whole team. There were 20 of us from various fields. My whole institute for forensic medicine and the huge number of people who accompanied him, I didn't know who they were in terms of their expertise. Ms. Marija Djuric talked to him I think -- well, she spoke to him as a colleague because they were both anthropologists. So we talked about all that, and I couldn't really give you an answer specifically whether this was discussed or not. I don't know. Well, there's one thing, there's the information that you receive in the field from the investigative organs, the investigative judge, the police, or the family members, if you talked to them, it's very important. And then you compare it with the post mortem changes that you determine. And then empirically you can see whether there are any discrepancies there. But any possible discrepancies in post mortem changes will depend on so many factors: The place where they were buried, the time when they were buried, the condition they were in before the transfer, whether they were exhumed there and then transferred here and then interred again. So we really don't know whether this was discussed at the meeting. I really don't know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please have on our screens 65 ter document 189 [as interpreted], it's a report, page 4 in B/C/S, and I believe it's page 5 in the English version. 65 ter document 179, it's a report -- [In English] It's not right number, 179, not 189.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now, I would like you to look at the Serbian version in B/C/S. Are you familiar with this document?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Now -- yeah, it's okay. Could you please look at what you wrote here and I would like us to look also at the conclusion in B/C/S for -- to assist the witness.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that there are several more items in the conclusion.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's on the next page, I believe.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know, do you remember the findings? There were many of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now I would like you to show page 1 to the witness in B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, do look at this too.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Fine.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: You know that this is Ba-12. The OMPF labelled the findings in the same way that you did.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now, I would like us to look at 5454 [as interpreted] page 22, or rather, P545 [as interpreted].

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Professor, do you speak or understand the English language?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do understand.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's page 22, please. Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: The same thing, it has to do with what you did. You see cause of death: Gun-shot to the head.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now, the same document, could you please take us to page 12. The page begins with a chart and then it goes on with paragraph 33, some examples. And I would like you to show just the bottom part starting with some examples and then all the way down to the photographs of the skull that we see here. So if we could zoom in on the lower part, 3.3.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Could you please look at this.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And now I would like you to show the next page, that would be page 13. Could you please zoom in -- yes, precisely on this part, yes. You can even zoom in even more because I'm more interested in the pictures of the skull.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Professor, this injury to the occipital bone, please don't take it amiss, I'm a layperson, if I misspoke, it is the obvious injury to the occipital bone. As an anthropologist, Baraybar puts it, it's a keyhole injury. And the conclusion is that this is a gun-shot wound, an entry and exit wound, from the above downwards. And now -- can you please comment this injury if possible.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I've read this, and I've seen this. We said that there were blunt trauma defects --

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: That's what you wrote?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This injury does have some features that could be attributed to an injury inflicted by a fire-arm; however, I couldn't really comment on this, on the comments made by Mr. Baraybar, for a simple reason, because I'm just a fact witness here and I can only testify to the fact to what we wrote. And I still stand by what we wrote. So I couldn't really comment on this. Now, as to what he said about the keyhole injury. As regards keyhole injuries, they are caused when there is a narrow angle of entry and a narrow angle of exit of the round, and there are some traces present at both ends. And I can only see some of them -- well, this is not something that you can use for an analysis, these are just photographs that we took. But the fracture that -- the fractures that were caused and that were observed earlier are ones that could have been caused by a blunt instrument. And that was the most proper conclusion. And now, if this injury was caused solely by a projectile that entered the head at such a narrow angle from the top and then went downwards, as a forensic scientist, as an expert, I would have to think really hard whether it was caused in this manner and whether it could actually have caused the death of this person, or whether other injuries that were found on other parts of the body were actually responsible for the death. In other words, in order to tell the Court why or how this person died, I have to have the consistency in my findings. In the autopsy findings, first of all, I don't have any reliable evidence that this was caused by fire-arms. I can see that there was a blunt trauma and that there was some artefacts caused by fire on the body and also that the body was putrefied. And now this has to be consistent with the findings and with the cause of death. Now, to claim that this was caused by a projectile because we have the keyhole injury and to the base of the skull at that, I would have a number of questions. And I would have to analyse this as an expert in order to give an answer. So to conclude, what we wrote, I stand by the conclusion in its entirety because we all analysed this injury and the previous injury where we saw the photograph with the defects, cause to the skull and caused by high temperature. Now as a witness I can just say that I stand by what I wrote and that's the only thing I stand by. As to his anthropological claim that this was caused by a projectile entering the skull at such and such an angle, well it's a bit outlandish. And also I have to tell you that this kind of injury could also have been caused by a pickaxe. You know a pickaxe, what it looks like, it has a flat part and the sharp part. This could also be done in the course of the exhumation, and we would have the same fractured ends as we see here; but I cannot claim that either, and I don't want to make this kind of analysis because I'm a fact witness here.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, but you're also an expert, but why didn't you then write, as Mr. Baraybar did, gun-shot to the head? That's what I'm asking you. You did the analysis and you signed it. So that's what I can ask you.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you can ask me --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: The speakers are kindly asked not to speak at the same time.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, we only wrote down what we are certain about. That's why we didn't write gun-shot wound, we said blunt injury.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Professor, I would like to thank you for sharing with us what you've told us. I think that this will be of great value for the truth in this case, and this is the most important thing for all of us here. And that is why I will thank you on my personal behalf for coming here and for telling us all you know about this. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, this concludes my cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUGGE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Djordjevic. Mr. Neuner, do you have any re-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: Just a few questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: You just -- good morning, first of all.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: You just mentioned it is possible that during exhumations certain wounds could be inflicted on a skull of a corpse which is lying in the ground which is to be explored. Could you just explain briefly what you meant?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You know, from this time distance, and it looks a bit odd at a first glance, but when you perform this kind of job in the field, you have to engage a large number of people and not all of them are physicians. You have forensic pathologists, archaeologists, but there were also technical staff, just like every other team, and you cannot supervise them all the time, 24 hours a day, and look what they're doing and how they're doing. Therefore, I say it is possible these things can happen during excavation. On the other hand, I don't know where a certain body had arrived from. Where had it been buried, how it was exhumed, how it was transported to Batajnica, these open up the possibilities --

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: I understand, there are other possibilities, but I'm only interested how members of your staff could have inflicted such a wound because you were suggesting it is possible.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I only said that it was possible. I'm not saying that they did that. I'm only telling you that there was such a possibility.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: Are you before you embark on an exhumation advising your staff how to behave in terms of exploring the grave so that such wounds on a skull could be avoided?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely, yes. Absolutely. But you have to know something: That was the first excavation of that magnitude in a single site ever carried out in Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: And did you advise, before you embarked with your staff on this exhumation, did you advise your staff to try to avoid such wounds?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The majority of the excavations were carried out by us, doctors, forensic experts, and anthropologists. Therefore, we made extreme efforts in order to keep everything intact. What I said was just the possibility --

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: Okay, okay --

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- that could indicate judging by the damage caused --

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: I was just asking whether you advised your staff, before they embarked on this particular exhumation, to engage in a practice which would not result into damaging skulls?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: And during the --

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I told them explicitly and I particularly focused on the skulls because this was the crucial point, not only in this particular case but I did the same in all the previous and subsequent cases as well. We have to be very precise.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: And while the work on Batajnica 1 and Batajnica 2 graves was going on, did at any point in time report one of your staff to you that he had engaged in some activity which could have caused the damage to a skull?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: I have some few questions relating to what you said this morning, and this is page 4 of today's transcript. You mentioned during the forensic examinations in Batajnica you had certain facts at your disposal and you were then listing three facts. One such fact was that the bodies had been buried before elsewhere. And I understood that to mean before the bodies came to Batajnica they had been buried elsewhere. Can you explain to me why did you think that this was a fact?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't consider that to be the case, but rather that this fact has to be incorporated in my mind as an expert and to direct my attention and try to look for the traces indicative of that and that could raise some suspicions in my mind that the bodies had been moved, that I would have to anticipate to see different types of injuries. And these were the facts that were conveyed by people in authority -- rather, by the court. And, after all, these people had been brought from somewhere to Batajnica. And I had to bear that in mind as a fact, that actually something had happened earlier down there and that I'm examining them here. And that in this interval between the point of their departure and their arrival, a lot of things could have happened that could have affected the post mortem findings. That was what I had in mind.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: Professor, you just mentioned that people in authority had mentioned that possibility or that fact to you. Could you tell me which people in authority were mentioning this to you?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I say "authority," the only authority that I am constantly in contact is the court, investigative court, and the investigative organs who are assisting us.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: And what did these investigative organs tell you about the possibility of a pre-burial?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was stories circulating around that the bodies had been buried in Kosovo prior to that, which I personally learned from my female fellow doctor who had been working at one of those locations, and on one locations in Batajnica, I'm not sure which ones, bodies were found in body-bags, if I'm not wrong.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: Was this in Batajnica 1 and 2, these two graves, if you remember?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: Can you give us the name of the female person who mentioned that to you, that pre-burial had occurred?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Dr. Gordana Tomasevic. She testified before this Court.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: Can you tell me as an expert being involved in exhumations for so many years, if a body has been buried in another mass grave or grave before and is transported to what I will call a secondary grave, are there any traces, such as earth or other items, which indicate to you that this body had been buried elsewhere?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: And which indications are these?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: These are the elements that indicate the composition of the earth if you find pieces of soil or artefacts found on the body or on the clothing of the body that can provide an explanation for the discrepancy between the two locations, especially between the original one from which the body had been brought and the new one.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: Were any members of your team, during the exhumations, looking for such traces? And I'm referring to the graves Batajnica 1 and 2.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Whatever we spotted and observed and believed to have found, we described that. We were primarily focused on describing the changes on the bones, the clothing, and the tissue that could be inconsistent with the ambience where the body was.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: Was at some point in time at the exhumations Batajnica 1 and 2 earth probes taken and compared with the local earth in order to establish whether there are different earth probes on the bodies?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We had a team of archaeologists who were working along with us analysing the soil in both Batajnica 1 and 2. These surveys and examinations were done.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: And do you know what the outcome of these examinations was by the archaeologists?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot tell you anything with any degree of certainty. All I know is that the composition of the soil in Batajnica 2, which was very sandy; however, in Batajnica 1 all the putrefied changes on the tissue and on the clothing created a matter around these bodies and the tissue changed to such an extent that it was impossible to establish whether it was caused by the putrefaction or by the soil from another location. We were not unable -- we were not able to establish this distinction. I believe that Batajnica 1 and Batajnica 2 were actually primary grave-sites for the majority of bodies, but I did have information that bodies had been exhumed, and I gave quite a lot of thought to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: And what information did you have that bodies were exhumed before they came to Batajnica?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Precisely what I just told you, information from the court that some of the bodies had been buried and were then exhumed and transported from that area to this area. I'm not saying that the judge himself said that and that my colleague corroborated it, but now when I'm giving evidence today I'm telling you what we were doing. But the impression was that the bodies in Batajnica 1 and Batajnica 2 were in primary graves. I'm not saying all of them, but the big majority of them. They didn't have this kind of changes in terms of soil or artefacts that will indicate that, because I had no idea where they had come from so I couldn't go down there and collect the artefacts and other clues in order to establish the facts, otherwise I don't have any reliable proof to that effect.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: You mentioned also on page 4 of today's transcript that bodies had been brought from elsewhere as a fact or an assumption. Why do you believe so?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Another option would be that they were killed there on the spot; however, we had all elements indicating that a large number of people were buried at the same time. Now, speaking from the forensic point of view, the information that the court had available and the investigating judge in particular was actually reliable information confirming that these bodies had been brought to this location from Kosovo, and these are two different things. Although one always thinks that it was possible for these people to be shot that -- and buried there; however, judging by the view, how they look, it is -- it was evident that this was a pile of bodies that was confined in one space and that was exhumed with bulldozers and then later on brought from Kosovo to this location. And that's all that I knew. That is precisely why identification not only of wounded but identification of people is so crucial, because it can establish a link between certain regions, geographical regions, and the people whose bodies were found.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: You mentioned the court had reliable information about the move of the bodies. Have you seen that information which the court possessed at the time?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I only had oral information.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: You mentioned - that is page 14 of today's transcript - that if somebody moves a dead body for a specific purpose that you could assume that this person could have shot at these dead bodies as well as in order to confuse the issue and therefore make it impossible for any anthropologist or pathologist to determine when the wound is inflicted on such a skeletonised body. And then you continued, So these things happened and I have such reports. Could you tell me which reports you were referring to?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is the information about the desecration of dead bodies committed by a certain group. What the KLA did, they used to kill their own people who did not agree with them or inflicted wounds subsequently. I heard that back in 1998 from many, many policemen and other security forces who were in Kosovo. I just wanted to draw your attention that there was a possibility for such tampering with the dead bodies, and of course, later on, this creates confusion for us forensic experts. First you move a body and then on the way you also shoot again at this pile of dead bodies, and then later on this will be portrayed as a complete massacre.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: Can you tell me if a body is moved for a couple of hundred kilometres to another location, how does this affect your work as a forensic pathologist in determining the cause of death?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It can have an impact in that the moving of the bodies from one location to another involves time, and thereby it increases the possibility of inflicting post mortem injuries and changes in terms of more advanced putrefaction. And they can conceal what happened before the death.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: Can you tell me if trucks are standing, following the move, for about two weeks before a grave -- before the bodies are put into a grave and buried finally, what effect does that have on the bodies and on you as a forensic expert who tries to find out the cause of death?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What trucks are you referring to?

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: I'm referring about trucks who were transporting bodies and who were standing for some two weeks before -- at a location before a grave is being dug and the bodies are --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Djordjevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Defence objection, Your Honour. This witness is being asked about the circumstances that this witness cannot answer. He's talking about trucks and other things. He can only ask him whether he knows how these bodies were transported. Therefore, I find this question to be leading.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Neuner.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: I also note the time. This was actually my final question. I only wanted to ask the perspective of a forensic pathologist because this witness mentioned that during the travel of bodies the decomposition of bodies continues, and I only wanted his assessment on the fact that if bodies still stay for two weeks somewhere before they are being buried, how that can affect the forensic analysis of the cause of death.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUGGE
utterances.text: Could you please answer this question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Since this is your last question, I am giving you the shortest possible answer: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: Okay. In the interests of time, the Prosecution has no questions, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Dunjic, we are pleased that you came to The Hague again. Thank you very much. And now this concludes the evidence you have to give to the Tribunal. Thank you very much. Now you are released and can go back to your ordinary activities. Thank you. We will have our break now and resume at five minutes past 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUGGE
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Stamp, is the next witness ready?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours. The next witness is Milos Deretic, and I think he's on his way. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUGGE
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUGGE
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Deretic. Could you please read aloud the affirmation on the card which is shown to you now.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours. I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUGGE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please sit down. I think Mr. Stamp has some questions for you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Your Honours. Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Deretic.

utterances.speaker: MILOS DERETIC
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Could we start by you introducing yourself to the Court, first your name, date of birth, occupation.

utterances.speaker: MILOS DERETIC
utterances.text: My name is Milos Deretic. I was born on the 18th of July, 1954, in Kosovo, in the place called Podujevo. From 1955 onwards, I was living in Pristina where I completed my elementary school, high school, and the faculty of electrical engineering. My major was in electronics and communications.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: What were you engaged in -- what was your job, put it that way, in 1998 and 1999?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DERETIC
utterances.text: From the 1st of February, 1982, I was working at the then-provincial SUP, Secretariat of Interior, in Pristina. In 1993 I was appointed chief of the communications sector in the Secretariat of the Interior in Pristina, and that is where I remained during 1998 and 1999.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: As chief of the communications sector in Pristina, what were your responsibilities, what did that job entail?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DERETIC
utterances.text: The communications sector of the Pristina SUP dealt with planning, development, and maintenance of communications systems in the area covered by the Pristina SUP. Pursuant to Article 45 of the rules on internal organisation of the Ministry of the Interior, our sector for communications had its scope of responsibilities and duties that they had to discharge for other secretariats in the area of Kosovo and Metohija. Therefore, it was practically responsible for the maintenance of communications systems for other secretariats in Kosovo and Metohija. Therefore, these involved regular activities of the Pristina SUP.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Could we, with your leave, Your Honour, have a look at document with the ERN number 01072.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: These are the rules establishing the internal organisation of the Ministry of the Interior.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Could we go to page 45 -- I'm sorry, I think we want Article 45 thereof. I'm not sure what the page number is. Yes, could we go to the last part of the next page.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Is this -- have you managed to look at it, Mr. Deretic? Is this the provision you were referring to?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DERETIC
utterances.text: You moved it a little bit. This is the analytics and IT sector. What we need is the communications and encryption sector. That's what we need on the screen. Could you please go to the previous page.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I think we need page 51 in English --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: You referred to Article 45, and I went along with that and had shown you Article 45.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: As a matter of fact, we want Article 46.

utterances.speaker: MILOS DERETIC
utterances.text: Yes, and it's probably at page 52 in the Serbian version. Could we please look at --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Could we please look at page 52 in the Serbian version.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I think in the last paragraph in the English version we see that it provided here that the secretariat in Pristina shall provide services in respect to communications for the territory of Kosovo and Metohija. Is this a provision on which you base your comment earlier, that you had responsibility for communications in all of Kosovo and Metohija?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BAIRD
utterances.text: Mr. Stamp, we haven't seen that on our monitor.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I'm so sorry. We need page 51, and that's the last part of Article 46. I'm so sorry, Your Honour. And I think we also need the next page in the B/C/S copy as well.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. That's it, but I was sure it was Article 45 but apparently it's Article 46. It says quite clearly here that the departments for communications and cryptographic protection in the secretariats in Novi Sad, Nis, and Pristina, and the sections for communications and cryptographic protection in the secretariat in Kraljevo shall also perform the tasks established above in the territory of other secretariats, the secretariats in Novi Sad and Pristina -

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: The witness is kindly asked to slow down when reading.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUGGE
utterances.text: I'm sorry. Could you please slow down a little bit. The interpreters don't get your reading out.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I'll do my best. So in this paragraph of Article 46 we see the definition of the obligation on the communications department to carry out certain tasks in the sphere of communications for other secretariats in Kosovo and Metohija.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: The rules for the internal organisation of the MUP, Your Honours, 0072 [sic], I would tender it and ask that it be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUGGE
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Stamp, the full document or only this part.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, the full document because it will be used again in the course of these case we don't want it to be piecemeal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUGGE
utterances.text: Okay it will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be P00584, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: During 1998 and 1999, was there an organ that was called the MUP staff for Kosovo and Metohija?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DERETIC
utterances.text: Well, I know that the MUP staff did exist, not only in 1998 and in 1999, but it existed as early as in 1993 when I became the head of the communications department. I know that the MUP staff existed at that time in Kosovo and Metohija.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Now, did you have -- did you have any responsibility in respect to the communications system, that served the MUP staff for Kosovo and Metohija?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DERETIC
utterances.text: Well, I can confirm that as of 1993, when I became the head of the communications department in the secretariat in Pristina, that under Article 46 we continuously provided technical support in a similar way to the MUP staff in Pristina, just as we made sure that the -- all communications systems in Kosovo and Metohija functioned. So this was our everyday routine obligation. We had those tasks as routine tasks, provision of technical support to the MUP staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Yes. Please remember to keep it slow. Thank you. Who was the head of the MUP staff in 1998 and 1999?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DERETIC
utterances.text: Well, I know that in 1998 it was General Sreten Lukic who was the head of the MUP staff in Pristina. So that was between mid-1998 and June 1999.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Now, the communications section of the Pristina SUP that you headed fell within which part of the organisational structure of the MUP?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DERETIC
utterances.text: Well, in the public security department in the ministry there was a communications administration as a territorial organisational unit. We, in the Pristina, secretariat were in that chain of command, so to speak, the cryptographic communications and protections. So the communications administration in the MUP headquarters had an obligation to provide professional support and to organise all communications in the Republic of Serbia. Its job description was -- it was supposed to plan, develop, modernise, and maintain all communications systems within the Republic of Serbia. The communications administration in the MUP headquarters was also charged with dealing with the training of the employees and drafting documents necessary for the operation of the communications equipment. As a territorial organisational unit, we, the communications sector, had to pursue the policy of the administration in the sphere of communications in our area of the secretariat of Pristina. And the organisational units in the sphere of communications were defined in the same way throughout Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Earlier you had discussed the MUP staff for Kosovo and Metohija. Were you ever a member of the MUP staff?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DERETIC
utterances.text: Yes, I was a member of the staff from the 1st of June, 1999, and then for the 15 or 20 days that followed, so over a very short time-period.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Did you attend any staff meetings?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DERETIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Could we bring up P67.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: The document of the 31st of May, 1999, and that is a decision on the establishment of the ministry staff. And before we go to the next page, you observe that in the middle of this page towards the end you are appointed the chief of signals. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Perhaps we can scroll down further --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Perhaps -- in the Serbian version I don't see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: It's the next page in the Serbian version.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, now I can see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And if we could quickly move to the end of the document, the last page of the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: We see that this is an order of the Minister Vlajko Stojiljkovic.

utterances.speaker: MILOS DERETIC
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Were you aware of this decision appointing you?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DERETIC
utterances.text: Yes, I received this decision, and as of the 1st of June, 1999, I did this work. At the same time I was head of the communications sector and at the same time I was the chief communications officer in the staff, so over this brief period of time it was my duty to gather and evacuate communications equipment from Kosovo and Metohija.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Prior to the NATO intervention of the 24th of March, 1999, can you briefly tell us what the communications system within Kosovo and Metohija or what sort of arrangements there were in respect to the communications system in Kosovo and Metohija.

utterances.speaker: MILOS DERETIC
utterances.text: Well, in line with the principle for the development defined by the ministry, the communications administration, there were elements of the communications system in Kosovo, integral parts of a single system. So we used, in Kosovo and Metohija, a telephone network. It was a special telephone network that was not open to public. It was the network used dedicated solely for the MUP. There was also a system to -- for the transfer of non-voice messages, telegraphic communications, in other words; there were radio systems that used UHF and VHF frequencies that were used by the ministry staff; and there was also a communications system using short-wave equipment. In regular circumstances, it was not used. They were only used -- this equipment was only used to check the working of the communications systems.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Could you tell us a little bit more about the telephone system. I take it from what you are saying there were two telephone systems in Kosovo at least, one available to the public at large and what you described as a special telephone network that was not open to the public. Can you tell us a little bit more about that special telephone network. Who was it open to and what was the level of security?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DERETIC
utterances.text: The special telephone network that you mention existed throughout the Republic of Serbia in the whole of the ministry, and it was set up in such a way that the telephone exchanges were placed in the buildings of all the secretariats. The telephone exchanges were linked in such a way that they formed a telephone network, and this telephone network, those telephone exchanges, rather, were used for the transmission of messages that were classified as highly confidential. What -- or were higher priority. What existed in Kosovo and Metohija was just part of this whole system that operated throughout the Republic of Serbia. So there was nothing there that didn't exist elsewhere in Serbia, and the network was set up in such a way that the exchanges were linked using telecom transmission systems. So in other words, the MUP did not have its own transmission systems, but it paid to the telecom for certain capacity to be able to link up the telephone exchanges. This network - and this is important when it was destroyed intentionally - was star-shaped and the centre was in Pristina.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And you also said there were radio systems that used UHF and VHF ministries and these were used by the ministry staff. Could you elaborate a little bit further. These radio systems enabled communications between which units or personnel of the MUP?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DERETIC
utterances.text: In line with the territorial organisation and the scope of the work of the ministry, the ministry set up the radio networks on the basis of the so-called territorial principle. So for each secretariat a network is set up using UHF range. It's 157 to 165 megahertz and this range used by MUP is defined in a document called the -- A Plan for the Distribution and Use of Frequencies which is in turn passed by the ministry of telecommunications at the state level. So in that UHF frequency, it is possible to establish communications between the secretariat headquarters and appropriate departments and police stations within that secretariat. So the communications are set up to meet the needs of one individual secretariat. In addition to that, in VHF ranges, in the towns within the secretariat area there is always the VHF network set up. It's between 440 and 456 megahertz, and this network is set up in order to maintain radio communications usually in the areas of towns and the immediate vicinity of towns. So these are the radio networks that the MUP used, so the situation was more or less the same in all the secretariats in Kosovo such networks were set up. Of course, since the coverage of a territory with radio signal depends on a number of factors, the lay of the land is one of the major factors, quite often additional radio networks were set up to meet the needs of some OUPs that could not get coverage from the regional networks.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: You mentioned a directory that was or a plan I think you called it. Called use of distribution and use of frequencies just passed by the Ministry of Communications at the state level. Were there also temporary directories of users of radio telecommunications links in the Kosovo and Metohija area?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DERETIC
utterances.text: Well, there has been a misunderstanding. The plan for use and distribution of radio frequencies, it is passed by the state, by the relevant ministry, the Ministry of Telecommunications, and the document is adopted by the government. And it defines the ranges for the police, for the military, for radio, for TV, and for all the other users of radio signals that exist in a state. I simply wanted to note that the MUP did not use radio frequencies that it felt like using, but only those that were allocated to it by this plan. So this is the plan for the use and distribution of frequencies. Now, directorates, it's a completely different story. In the ministry, in order for the radio communications to be maintained in an appropriate manner, there must be regulations. The ministry had the instruction for the use of radio and telephone system of the MUP of the Republic of Serbia. An integral part of the instruction was the so-called directory of users of radio and telephone systems.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Could we -- thank you. Before you go on --

utterances.speaker: MILOS DERETIC
utterances.text: Which --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Could we bring up 65 ter number 01071.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And if you could just have a look at this document and then you could finish your answer.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreters would be grateful if the witness could be asked to slow down. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Mr. Deretic, if you could remember to speak slowly. The interpreters are having some difficulty. I think you have seen this document before, but if we could just scroll through it quickly.

utterances.speaker: MILOS DERETIC
utterances.text: Yes, I was shown this in a previous trial. I can see just the front page in the Serbian version.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Could we move to the next page in Serbian version.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Could you just tell us briefly, very briefly, what the document is about and what its purpose is.

utterances.speaker: MILOS DERETIC
utterances.text: This kind of document is used when there are various security actions. As for this specific document, I don't know about that, because this is -- actually the first time I saw this document was at the Milutinovic trial. It does present the regular channels with the call-signs for various secretariats. So it is an excerpt from the directory of the users of radio and telephone systems, so all members of the Pristina SUP have the call-sign Sitnica and they work at channel 58. And then all the secretariats in Kosovo and Metohija are listed here. So I can say that this is a good document and all the channels, the regular channels listed here, are accurate.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: You were just referring to the section of this document under the heading "regular channels."

utterances.speaker: MILOS DERETIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And if we could move on. Are you aware of the -- or perhaps you could tell us this: What were radio call-signs, if you could describe that quickly.

utterances.speaker: MILOS DERETIC
utterances.text: Well, the directory of the users of radio and telephone systems defines all general call-signs for various secretariats so that the call-signs listed here, Sitnica, Ibar, Bistrica, Drim, Sara, Breza, and Cer, are indeed the call-signs for all the members of the secretariats as they're listed here respectively.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I think the witness is now referring to items that are on the first page of the English, so if you could go back to the first page of the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And would personnel within each SUP use the same call-sign?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DERETIC
utterances.text: That's correct. The call-signs of the users of radio communications contains the general call-sign, Sitnica, and a figure, one-digit, double-digit, or triple-digit figure or it can go even up to five digits. So I can say that I was Sitnica 601, that was my call-sign when using radio communications because I was a member of the Pristina SUP and in this capacity I used it.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Did the special units, police units, in Kosovo, the SAJ, the JSO, and the PJP, did they have their own call-signs?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DERETIC
utterances.text: Naturally. All participants in radio communications, in order to use radio communications, had to use their call-signs. That was a rule. Every participant must identify himself using the call-sign.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Do you remember the call-signs for those units that I just mentioned?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DERETIC
utterances.text: Well, I don't know specifically for SAJ and JSO. I know that there were Sigma, Delta, Cegar, those were some of the call-signs that were used, Koseva, Munja, Soko.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: If we could move to the last page of this document in English, and it's also the last page, I think, in B/C/S. And this is under the heading "code tables."

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Could you explain to us what was the -- what is the meaning of what we see here?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DERETIC
utterances.text: This is a standard encoded table of codes that the police used because radio communications of the ministry were constantly being intercepted or jammed by the Albanian separatists. The reason was because all the radio communications were established in the so-called analog technology and it was easy to eavesdrop and jam them. In order for the police to convey a message without its being intercepted by hostile parties, then this table of codes was used to convey this message in a way that the other party would not be able to understand it. This table of codes was a combination of colours and numbers which sort of indicated the state in which a unit or an individual was. For example, Grey 1 meant: I have a wounded man. Grey 5 meant: I have dead men. Red 2 indicated: Expecting an attack.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Could this document, Your Honours, be given an exhibit number? It's 65 ter number --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUGGE
utterances.text: Yes, it will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be P00585, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUGGE
utterances.text: What about the last document we have had earlier?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: P -- P67. I think it was already --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUGGE
utterances.text: It's already in evidence. Carry on, Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: You referred to a third method of communication that occurred prior to the NATO interventions and that was telegraphic transfers. Briefly, could you tell us how that system worked in Kosovo and Metohija prior to the NATO intervention.

utterances.speaker: MILOS DERETIC
utterances.text: The telegraphic system was used for conveyance of official written messages or dispatches as they're also called. It is set up in a similar way as a telephone network. There are the so-called telegraphic interconnected exchanges; and by using telegraphic codes, they convey official written messages to the ministry, from the secretariat to the ministry. What we had in Kosovo was also part of a single telegraphic system set up in the entire territory of Kosovo and Metohija -- I'm sorry, in the entire territory of the Republic of Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: So the telegraphic system enabled you to communicate via messages within Kosovo and also outside of Kosovo too, for example, the ministry headquarters in Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DERETIC
utterances.text: That's right. Each secretariat was capable of communicating with any other secretariat and, naturally, with the headquarters of the ministry as well. That of course refers to the period prior to the bombing.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Now, you mentioned dispatches. Is there a format or official requirement of a dispatch as understood within the terminology of the MUP?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DERETIC
utterances.text: I can only give you a definition of what a dispatch is.
