It is an official message drafted and prepared for communication via technical means; and its format is such that it contains the heading, the address of the recipient, the contents, and the signature of the sender. So there's nothing special to it as far as the format is concerned.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: As -- having regard to your role in the MUP, can you recognise or identify dispatches by their appearance?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DERETIC
utterances.text: In the course of communication and in the course of sending and transmitting dispatches, only the sender and the recipient are entitled to see it. I, as the chief of the communications sector, had no right to review any dispatch that was sent by technical means of communication.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Did your section or did you have cause at any time to send dispatches?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DERETIC
utterances.text: Yes. The communications section of course sent its own dispatches to other organisational units within the ministry.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And would those dispatches that you have said conform to the requirements for dispatches that you just described earlier?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DERETIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes, by all means.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you. We'll return to dispatches a little later. The -- let's turn to the NATO intervention. Did the telephone system of communications that existed in Kosovo prior to the NATO intervention remain intact during the NATO intervention?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DERETIC
utterances.text: No. When the bombing started as early as towards the end of March, more precisely on the 29th of March, the Pristina SUP building was demolished which also housed the main telephone exchange. Therefore, this made any telephone communication between the Pristina SUP and Belgrade through our special network was made impossible. The only intact part was public telephony and public telephone numbers that were still operational. Of course, during the bombing campaign, transmission sites were constantly targeted in Kosovo and Metohija. They contained the radio equipment of the MUP, of the army, and they were also used -- these installations were also used by telecom company where their transmission systems were housed. For example, Goles was demolished already in late March. It is situated some 20 kilometres from Pristina. After that, the transmission systems belonging to Telekom, which is the public telephony company, ceased to be operable, which also eliminated the possibility to use this public telephony in Metohija -- particularly Pec, Djakovica, and Prizren and also Gnjilane. At the moment when Goles was demolished, all these towns in Kosovo and Metohija could not receive any dispatches, I mean the secretariats in those towns. There was also no public telephony available. The only towns that we could communicate with were Urosevac and Mitrovica because these towns were connected by coaxial cables. However, soon after, I think it was on the 6th of April, 1999, the building of Telekom company in Pristina was hit. It was called telecommunications centre 2. In this building were all public transmissions systems housed. After this building was destroyed, there was no public telephony at all in Kosovo and Metohija. The only communication lines went from Pristina to Nis and Belgrade because it was done through an optical cable, particularly the one from Nis to Pristina, and that was the only operating line of communication at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: The -- this optical cable that enabled communication from Pristina to Nis and Belgrade, was this part of the police system or part of the public telephone system?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DERETIC
utterances.text: I already said that the police didn't have their own transmission system, neither optical nor radio relay. We leased these facilities from the Telekom company, so this optical cable was actually belonging to Telekom as a public operator in both fixed and mobile telephony.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: The -- this optical cable system, did it remain available to the police during the intervention?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DERETIC
utterances.text: Not only to the police. It was used for public traffic, public telephony traffic as well. We only used these telephone connections and the possibility to make telephone calls to Belgrade and Nis and so on and so forth. This cable was operational during the war with some exceptions. It was damaged on two occasions which resulted in the severance of communications that lasted for two days on each occasion. One of the damages was in the village of Luzane, when a bus full of civilians was hit near Podujevo. And therefore, since this optical cable was damaged, it prevented any communication in the area or from the area of Kosovo and Metohija.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: How long did that interruption last, do you recall?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DERETIC
utterances.text: I think for a couple of days. I cannot tell you exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Were there -- were mobile telephones operational in Kosovo during the NATO intervention?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DERETIC
utterances.text: All I know is that one mobile station of Mobtel company was operating in the area of town, but it had a very limited range. It covered only the urban area of the town or the centre of the town and nothing more than that. Because all the transmitters were demolished and there was no way of installing new equipment there because the entire actually infrastructure was destroyed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: So in terms of the telephone availability to the MUP during the war, there was just the limited availability of the mobile within the town centre as well as the line to Nis and Belgrade. Was there any other telephone system available or was that it?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DERETIC
utterances.text: Mobile telephones were operational within the very centre of Pristina. There was one regional telephone exchange in operation, in the so-called new post office, through which calls could be placed to other parts of Serbia but only from Pristina.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Which takes me to the next question. The other seven SUPs in Kosovo and Metohija -- sorry, the other six SUPs, there being seven in all, did they have access to telephone connections primarily with Belgrade during the intervention?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DERETIC
utterances.text: No, no. When I was explaining these transmissions system, I don't know if I am making it clear when I'm speaking of transmission systems. In order, for example, for vehicles to be able to road, you need roads. These transmission systems actually are telecommunication highways set up to provide for all the messages from one -- from A to B to arrive. If you don't have a highway, you cannot send any messages or voice data or anything. So in the aftermath of the destruction of the telecom building in Pristina, all these transmission systems and the equipment that was housed therein were destroyed and it was irreparable. There was a total cut-off of communications. It was impossible to communicate with the secretariats in Kosovo and Metohija and Pristina and vice versa. The only communication from Kosovo was possible with Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Did the -- was the situation any different in respect to radio communications and telegraphic communications?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DERETIC
utterances.text: Radio communications that were used by the ministry were also practically destroyed because the repeaters that supported these radio communications were installed at transmission locations which were practically destroyed during the NATO bombing. Those were Butovacki Breg near Pristina; Goles that I mentioned earlier; Stari Trg near Mitrovica; Mokra Gora near Zubin Potok; Cabrat near Djakovica; Cviljan near Prizren; Zeleni Vrh near Gnjilane; Prepolac near Podujevo. So these were the sites where MUP had their own equipment. Once they were destroyed, the equipment was destroyed too and there was no radio communication available in the manner that it was possible prior to the bombing.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Approximately when were these radio relay stations destroyed? I think you called them repeaters, repeaters that supported the radio station. About when were they destroyed?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DERETIC
utterances.text: I said about Goles, although I don't have the exact dates, because all of these sites were targeted several times. As early as the end of March was destroyed, and I know that because it was a very important hub for all the users. And I believe that sometime by mid-April all these transmission installations were destroyed and rendered unusable.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: How, then during the intervention, did the SUPs outside of Pristina and the units in the field in Kosovo and Metohija communicate with Belgrade -- sorry, with the MUP staff in Pristina and the secretariat in Pristina? And this is during the NATO intervention.

utterances.speaker: MILOS DERETIC
utterances.text: The police and our services did their best to establish some sort of radio network in towns, but we couldn't use some dominant location that could enable us to cover wider territory. We could only cover towns. Under such circumstances, it was no longer possible to establish direct communication between the secretariats and Pristina, and I mean direct radio communication.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: In the field, the units on the ground in the field, did they have short-wave radio systems that they could use amongst themselves?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DERETIC
utterances.text: Well, short-wavelength systems were mostly in the headquarters of the secretariats. During the war and NATO bombing, this equipment was practically out of use for a very simple reason, that everybody was afraid that if this installation were switched on it would easily be detected and become a target of aerial bombing. So people were in panic, people who were directly working on these equipments, radio telegraph operators, communications officers and others who were supposed to send a message, they were extremely weary of working on these machines and sending machines. Therefore, I cannot tell you exactly whether any messages were sent or if any were sent.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And were there hand-held radios - we have heard them being referred to as Motorolas - used in the field?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DERETIC
utterances.text: Hand-held radio sets were used the whole time but in a so-called simplex mode of operation. That involves a direct link between several sets; however, the range either depending on the configuration of the terrain is limited to not more than several kilometres. If they use so-called semi-duplex mode of operations, then a repeater is installed at a high elevation and it actually convoys voice and radio messages between two end users. If there is no repeaters or if they are destroyed, then the range of this kind of radio communication is very limited. Because radio waves generated within these ranges stretch along the line of optical visibility, and in the event of some obstacle existing between the two users, the radio waves deflect or reflect this obstacle. That is why I underline the importance of the so-called simplex mode of operation.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Do you know if any of these short-wave -- sorry, of these hand-held radio systems operated in duplex mode during the NATO intervention?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DERETIC
utterances.text: They could have been used and they were most probably used by using a repeater; but in that situation, no one can guarantee any wide coverage. The repeater was then probably at some lower elevation, and it could only cover some small territory through this mode of operation. So again, a problem would arise how to communicate with a detachment in the field with Pristina depending, of course, if between Pristina and the location where the unit is deployed is some kind of obstacle. So unless a repeater is installed on a high elevation, like the ones I mentioned before, like Goles, Cviljan, and other which are actually high hills, one could not count on good coverage of radio signal and communications.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, apart from the availability or limited availability of technical means of communication, can you tell us how otherwise did the secretariats and units in the field in Kosovo communicate with the headquarters in Pristina, the MUP staff in Pristina?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DERETIC
utterances.text: I can only assume that they used couriers who carried messages, but I cannot confirm that with any degree of certainty because the courier service was not within the scope of responsibility of my sector. It was attached to some other organisational units.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Which organisational unit was the courier sector attached to?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DERETIC
utterances.text: As far as I know, they were part of the general affairs sector of each secretariat. There was a group of people who constituted this sector and also the vehicle pool was also part of that sector, and they used to carry post and mail to Belgrade as well. I think they belonged to the general or joint affairs sector who were responsible for the courier service as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: About how often would they carry mail to and from Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DERETIC
utterances.text: I cannot give you a reliable confirmation. Perhaps it depended on the specific circumstances or the needs. They went probably a few times a week, but I cannot say for sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. Do you know whether or not the -- on the line that existed to Nis and Belgrade, that is, the telephone line, the optic cable, there were any numbers that were reserved, that is telephone numbers that were reserved, for the use of some police personnel or some person of the MUP?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DERETIC
utterances.text: Well, the question is not clear to me. We did use telephone numbers that were part of the public system everywhere. Now, whether those numbers were reserved -- well, I can't see why they should be because the Telekom has a large number of numbers and it has a vested interest in selling as many numbers as possible to reap the profits from the telephone traffic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Well, in the circumstances that prevailed during the NATO intervention, do you know if any of the numbers were reserved for use by the MUP or MUP personnel?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DERETIC
utterances.text: Well, I can say that as regards the Pristina SUP, in addition to the systems -- well, even in regular day-to-day business, numbers from public telephone exchanges were used. They were used at all times by the secretariat staff, and they continued to be used in the period that followed. And it is only -- well, because there was a telephone exchange in the building that was destroyed and that telephone exchange was also destroyed or damaged, then the numbers were simply rerouted from another telephone exchange. So whenever was entitled to use the public telephone system in Pristina could use it, and they were able to use it before the air-strikes, during the air-strikes, with the exceptions of the parts of town where the cable network had been destroyed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you. I'd like to show you a few documents and ask you whether or not these documents are in the standard format of dispatches sent by the public security sector of the ministry.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Could we bring up 04093. On the -- I should indicate just for the record that this document has already been admitted in evidence as P131.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Can you describe this document in terms of your understanding as to what a dispatch should consist of, a MUP dispatch should consist of.

utterances.speaker: MILOS DERETIC
utterances.text: Well, this is the format of the document that could be sent using technical communications equipment in the form of a dispatch; in other words, there is the heading and the address of the addressee. And if I could look at page 2, just the end of the dispatch, the signature --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUGGE
utterances.text: Just a moment. Mr. Djordjevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: One moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think that the witness cannot testify as to the contents of this document, and that is why -- and he has never seen this document before. And this is why I object to this line of questioning unless the witness is directly involved in the drafting and the contents of this document. So that would be my objection, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Your Honour, that is one element that can be considered for the purpose of admitting the document, but if the witness, from his own experience as a police officer involved in communications, can identify the format of the document as being the -- being a dispatch, a MUP dispatch, then it could be admitted on that basis.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Djordjevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's not a problem with the admission of the document. As my learned friend has just said, this has already been admitted into evidence. The problem is questioning the witness about something that, to my mind, the witness definitely cannot answer in this manner, because this is a document that he should testify about as to its form, not the contents. So I don't see the purpose of this line of questioning, but it is of course up to you to decide.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Yes, if I ...

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: As indicated by counsel for the Defence, the document is already admitted. The question really is to the form, whether this document is in the format of dispatches for the MUP.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUGGE
utterances.text: The Chamber is of the view that you should continue your questioning in that way.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Your Honour. Perhaps, with the leave of the Court, I could hand the witness a hard copy since he would like to look at both sides of the document.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. With the caveat that I have never seen this document, the only thing I can say is that this is a document that could be transmitted in the form of a dispatch. I can confirm that, but it is a document that does not contain details that a dispatch should have; in other words, some kind of a confirmation that it was transmitted using communications equipment. When it is done, then there should be a signature of persons who actually did the transmitting in technical terms.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: You said that this is a document that could be transmitted in the form of a dispatch. Could you just explain what you mean, having regard to the system that was in place.

utterances.speaker: MILOS DERETIC
utterances.text: Well, I told you what a dispatch is. A dispatch is an official message. Every official message that is written down can be transmitted using communications equipment in the following way: An operator, using the telegram system, types up the message brought by the person sending the message and then forwards it to wherever it has to go. So the dispatch does not have to have a special format. Every official message that reaches a communications operator to be transmitted using communications equipment is a dispatch.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: When a document is prepared, for example, that one that you have to be sent as a dispatch, after the dispatch is sent is that document filed or stored in any archive?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DERETIC
utterances.text: It is not archived in our sector, but every dispatch that has been forwarded sent with a copy thereof, and the original is returned to the sender. In the communications sector, we did not have an archive. We would always return the dispatch, give it back to the sender.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Your Honours, I was about to move to a set of documents, and I'm wondering if perhaps we could take the technical break five minutes earlier so that I could organise the documents more -- in a more presentable fashion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUGGE
utterances.text: Very well. Then we will have our break now and resume at five minutes to 1.00.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I'm grateful, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUGGE
utterances.text: Please, Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: How did your sector or your unit communicate with the MUP headquarters in Belgrade during the NATO intervention?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DERETIC
utterances.text: In view of the fact that the ministry building, sometime in early April, was bombed and destroyed, on that occasion the telecommunications room where the majority of equipment of -- for communication was housed was burned. So we were faced with a problem of how to organise this communications system. So most of the time, I communicated with the ministry on public telephony because there were no other communications lines because this main special switchboard or exchange was burned as well in that communications room that was used previously for all these special lines that went to the ministry.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: When you said most of the times you used the telephone system. On other occasions, what means did you to use to communicate with the headquarters in Belgrade apart from the telephone system?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DERETIC
utterances.text: Well, in the period preceding the bombing, it was possible to use a telegraphic system to send dispatches. We also had this special telephone network, so calls could have been made or could be made through that special telephone network as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I'm talking about the period during the bombing. If you had documents that you needed to send to Belgrade or they needed to send to you, how would that be sent?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DERETIC
utterances.text: Most often we used Telefax machines connected to a public telephone line.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And if there were problems within the telephone systems in Kosovo and Metohija itself, how would you be able to communicate with the people who operated the system in the various other areas or SUPs in Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DERETIC
utterances.text: All I can say about this issue is how I and my communications sector communicated with other SUP communications sectors. They would come over to fetch either equipment or to ask for advice. They came in person so they acted as some sort of couriers. They took whatever they needed, which means that I was not communicating with them, either via radio or via telephone.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: As far as the courier system was concerned, do you -- are you aware of the amount of vehicles that was available to the car pool in Pristina for the courier service within Kosovo and to Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DERETIC
utterances.text: I really don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Your Honours, that is all in chief. I had put down some documents for this witness, but having considered over the break it might be more convenient to tender them at a later time through someone else. So I have nothing further in chief. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Very well. Mr. Djordjevic, do you have some cross-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will surely have some questions during cross-examination; however, I wonder whether it would be better for me to do it tomorrow morning because after I had a conversation with my client I concluded that it would be necessary for me to obtain some documents that I hopefully will obtain during this afternoon. For the sake of consistency of my entire cross-examination, I believe that at this point it would be wiser for us to adjourn for today and then tomorrow morning I can finish very quickly. This is particularly in view of the need for me to obtain this document, and my client fully agreed with that.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will really need very little time for the cross-examination - I wanted to underline that - not more than half an hour, maybe even less.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUGGE
utterances.text: I think the problem is that we lose quite a lot of time, 40 minutes, and we -- as you know, we all try and have to try and speed up the proceedings. Therefore, it's the question if you can perhaps just start with your cross-examination and continue tomorrow. That would be helpful, then you have I think enough time to prepare the cross-examination with some new documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I actually have nothing else to ask this witness about apart from this document. I have no other questions for him. If only I can find this document, then will I be able to ask the questions. I tried to get hold of it during the break; however, I failed. Therefore, my only questions are about this document or, more precisely, a dispatch that I will do my best to locate. If I fail to do that, then I will have no questions for this witness and I have high hopes that I will be able to obtain this document. That's all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Djordjevic, the Chamber is of the view that it would be perhaps unfair not to adjourn now and to give you the chance to collect these documents; on the other hand, could you perhaps explain why it was not possible to get these information -- these documents earlier because if that happens more often we would have a problem in future.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, we've been together in this courtroom from the very beginning and you understand that this is the first time that something like this has happened. This issue arose from today's direct examination. My client recalled a 1997 dispatch which speaks about the lines of work, and we believe that this is crucially important for the Defence case. Originally we thought that this question should not be raised before this Trial Chamber, but since my client definitely remembers this dispatch and that we believe that after this document has been put to the witness two or three questions will be conducive to solving some very important issues. That is the reason why this happened as it has. Rest assured that this is not an excuse for us to waste time, quite the contrary. We are here with the same feeling and ambition that we should work effectively and efficiently. However, I did this for the sake of justice, and I believe that I will be able to obtain this until tomorrow morning. If I weren't sure of that, then I wouldn't make this commitment; otherwise, I really wouldn't like to see this witness go and then be called to appear again within six months' time, because as I said, I'm sure I will get hold of this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUGGE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Djordjevic. Mr. Stamp, have you any comment?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: No, Your Honours, I'm entirely in the hands of the Court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Djordjevic, you will be pleased to hear that you have even more time to prepare the cross-examination because we are sitting in the afternoon tomorrow and not in the morning. And so the Chamber is of the view that we should adjourn now and resume tomorrow in the afternoon. Sorry that we have to -- have to have a break now and continue the examination tomorrow. Thank you very much and then we adjourn now.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Tuesday, the 7th day of April, 2009, at 2.15 p.m. 21 22 23 24 25
